## Supplementary @suppfig-sensitivity-combinations: Exact Intervention Combinations and Their Constituent Interventions

::::: {#suppfig-sensitivity-combinations suppfig-align="left"}

```{r}
#| fig-align: left
#| out-width: "100%"
#| echo: false

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("Output", "Forest_plots", "sensitivity_combinations_forest_plot.png"))
```

**Exact intervention combinations and their constituent interventions: an exploratory sensitivity analysis.** Forest plot showing average treatment effects (ATEs) on DunedinPACE for the `r n_top_combinations` most frequent exact-use combinations containing at least two interventions (@suppfig-upset), together with the `r n_component_interventions` individual interventions occurring in those combinations. The individual-intervention rows repeat the corresponding estimates from the main pharmacological intervention forest plot (@fig-forest-plot-treatments); other main-analysis interventions are omitted. Combination rows require use of every listed intervention and no use of the remaining interventions among the 18 evaluated, and compare these participants with all remaining participants. The individual-intervention rows compare users with non-users and include concurrent users. The purpose is to explore whether common combinations have more favorable estimated associations with the pace of biological aging than their constituent intervention exposures. Both inverse probability weighting (IPW) and G-computation use the main analytical cohort and adjust for the same covariates. Circles represent point estimates and capped horizontal lines represent 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; the dashed vertical line indicates no effect. All rows are ordered together by the signed IPW estimate, from most negative to most positive. ATE percentages and their 95% confidence limits express absolute DunedinPACE differences as percentages of the reference pace of 1 biological year per calendar year. Divide the displayed ATE percentage and each confidence limit by 100, retaining their signs, to recover absolute differences in DunedinPACE units.

:::::

```{r}
    `Exposure type` = exposure_type,
    `ATE (IPW)` = sprintf("%.2f%%", ate_estimate_ipw * 100),
    `CI (IPW)` = sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", ci_lower_ipw * 100, ci_upper_ipw * 100),
    `Residual imbalance` = format_residual_imbalance(SMD, treatment, analysis),
    `ATE (G-comp)` = sprintf("%.2f%%", ate_estimate_std * 100),
    `CI (G-comp)` = sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", ci_lower_std * 100, ci_upper_std * 100),
    `N Exposed` = n_treated_ipw,
    `N Reference` = n_control_ipw
  )

register_supplementary_table(supplementary_export, "supptbl-sensitivity-combinations",
                             sensitivity_combinations_comparison_table)
```

## Supplementary @suppfig-heatmap-ipw: Standardized Biomarker Estimates Using IPW

::::: {#suppfig-heatmap-ipw suppfig-align="left"}

```{r}
#| fig-align: left
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(biomarker_output_dir, "main_heatmap_IPW.png"))
```

**Standardized biomarker estimates using inverse probability weighting (IPW).** Cells show adjusted average treatment effects for intervention use versus non-use and exercise-frequency categories versus never exercising. Columns represent biomarkers and rows represent interventions. All biomarkers except DunedinPACE were regressed on chronological age and the residuals standardized before modeling, yielding estimates in age-adjusted SD units. DunedinPACE was standardized directly without age residualization, retaining the main-analysis method apart from standardization before IPW and G-computation. Green denotes negative and red positive displayed ATE estimates, with white at zero and color saturation at ±`r heatmap_export_metadata$heatmap_limit`. For Telomere.Values.PC and DNAmVO2max (†), original estimates are multiplied by −1 for both colors and clustering. Green therefore indicates a favorable estimate direction in these biomarkers. Dendrograms show Euclidean-distance, complete-linkage clustering of the full sign-adjusted profiles, independently for each axis. A cell star (*) indicates that the original 95% bootstrap confidence interval strictly excludes zero, without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Original estimates, confidence intervals, displayed values, sample sizes and actual bootstrap counts are provided in Supplementary Data S1.

:::::

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(biomarker_output_dir, "main_heatmap_G-comp.png"))
```

**Standardized biomarker estimates using G-computation.** Cells show adjusted average treatment effects for intervention use versus non-use and exercise-frequency categories versus never exercising. Columns represent biomarkers and rows represent interventions. All biomarkers except DunedinPACE were regressed on chronological age and the residuals standardized before modeling, yielding estimates in age-adjusted SD units. DunedinPACE was standardized directly without age residualization, retaining the main-analysis method apart from standardization before IPW and G-computation. Green denotes negative and red positive displayed ATE estimates, with white at zero and color saturation at ±`r heatmap_export_metadata$heatmap_limit`. For Telomere.Values.PC and DNAmVO2max (†), original estimates are multiplied by −1 for both colors and clustering. Green therefore indicates a favorable estimate direction in these biomarkers. Dendrograms show Euclidean-distance, complete-linkage clustering of the full sign-adjusted profiles, independently for each axis. A cell star (*) indicates that the original 95% bootstrap confidence interval strictly excludes zero, without adjustment for multiple comparisons. ## Supplementary @suppfig-subgroup-sex: Effects of Pharmacological Interventions on DunedinPACE – Subgroup Analysis for Men vs Women

::::: {#suppfig-subgroup-sex suppfig-align="left"}

```{r}
#| fig-align: left
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 9.91
#| echo: false

load(here::here("Output", "Forest_plots", "subgroup_sex_forest_plot"))
plot
```

**Subgroup analysis in men versus women.** Forest plot showing average treatment effects (ATEs) of the evaluated pharmacological interventions on DunedinPACE among men compared to women. **(A)** Inverse probability weighting (IPW). **(B)** G-computation. Each panel overlays men and women, with the same intervention order and effect scale in both panels. Circles represent point estimates and capped horizontal lines represent 95% confidence intervals; the dashed vertical line indicates no effect (ATE = 0). The figure was used to assess whether intervention effects differed by biological sex. ATE percentages and their 95% confidence limits express absolute DunedinPACE differences as percentages of the reference pace of 1 biological year per calendar year. Divide the displayed ATE percentage and each confidence limit by 100, retaining their signs, to recover absolute differences in DunedinPACE units.

## Supplementary @supptbl-subgroup-men

::::: {#supptbl-subgroup-men supptbl-align="left"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
#| cache: false

# Load both subgroup results for men
load(here::here("Output", "IPW_subgroup_male_df"))
load(here::here("Output", "Standardization_subgroup_male_df"))

# Prepare IPW results
ipw_male_formatted <- IPW_subgroup_male_df |>
  mutate(
    SMD = format_residual_imbalance(SMD, treatment, "subgroup_male"),
    Treatment = treatment,
    `ATE (IPW)` = sprintf("%.2f%%", ate_estimate * 100),
    `95% CI (IPW)` = sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", ci_lower * 100, ci_upper * 100),
    ipw_ate = ate_estimate
  ) |>
  select(Treatment, `ATE (IPW)`, `95% CI (IPW)`, SMD, ipw_ate)

# Prepare Standardization results
std_male_formatted <- Standardization_subgroup_male_df |>
  mutate(
    Treatment = treatment,
    `ATE (G-comp)` = sprintf("%.2f%%", ate_estimate * 100),
    `95% CI (G-comp)` = sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", ci_lower * 100, ci_upper * 100)
  ) |>
  select(Treatment, `ATE (G-comp)`, `95% CI (G-comp)`)

# Merge results side by side and sort by IPW effect estimate
male_comparison_table <- ipw_male_formatted |>
  left_join(std_male_formatted, by = "Treatment") |>
  mutate(
    `N Treated` = IPW_subgroup_male_df$n_treated,
    `N Control` = IPW_subgroup_male_df$n_control,
    `Balance (SMD)` = SMD
  ) |>
  arrange(ipw_ate) |>
  select(Treatment, `ATE (IPW)`, `95% CI (IPW)`, `Balance (SMD)`,
         `ATE (G-comp)`, `95% CI (G-comp)`,
         `N Treated`, `N Control`) |>
  rename(
    `CI (IPW)` = `95% CI (IPW)`,
    `CI (G-comp)` = `95% CI (G-comp)`,
    `Residual imbalance` = `Balance (SMD)`,
    `N Users` = `N Treated`,
    `N Non-users` = `N Control`
  )

# Apply display names to Treatment column
male_comparison_table <- male_comparison_table |>
  mutate(Treatment = sapply(Treatment, format_display_name)) |>
  rename(Intervention = Treatment)

# Display the men subgroup comparison table as a flextable
male_comparison_table_flextable <- flextable(male_comparison_table) |>
  fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
  padding(padding = 2, part = "all") |>
  autofit() |>
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1, align = "left")

# Print the flextable
male_comparison_table_flextable

register_supplementary_table(supplementary_export, "supptbl-subgroup-men", male_comparison_table)
```

Full table, title, and caption: see the accompanying supplementary tables Excel workbook.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("Output", "love_plots", "subgroup_female", "love_plot_Antiaging_Hormone_Replacement.png"))
```

**Covariate balance for hormone replacement therapy in women.** Love plot showing standardized mean differences (SMDs) for demographic and lifestyle covariates before and after inverse probability weighting (IPW). The dashed vertical lines at \|SMD\| = 0.1 indicate the conventional threshold for adequate balance. Positive SMDs indicate higher values for continuous covariates or higher proportions in the listed categories among women using HRT compared with women not using HRT; negative SMDs indicate lower values for continuous covariates or lower proportions in the listed categories among women using HRT compared with women not using HRT. Notably, chronological age remained imbalanced after IPW, with more users being older.
